hints: Start by thinking about the two pieces of DNA you need to join - the bacterial herbicide-resistance gene and the carrier DNA that will take it into the soybean cell.
Recall which enzyme acts like molecular scissors to cut DNA at specific sequences, and what kind of ends it leaves for joining.
Think about which enzyme does the opposite joining job to seal the foreign gene into the opened plasmid to make recombinant DNA.
Remember that a bacterial gene alone will not work in a plant cell unless it has a control switch next to it - what is that regulatory sequence called?
Link that regulatory sequence to its job in transcription, so the new gene is actually switched on and makes protein in the soybean.
walkthrough:
Cutting Out the Wanted Gene**
Think of the bacterial herbicide-resistance gene as a paragraph you want to cut out and paste elsewhere. Restriction endonuclease is the scissors that cuts DNA at a specific recognition sequence. Here it cuts out the bacterial gene and it also cuts open the plasmid vector in the same way, so the ends match.

Pasting to Make Recombinant DNA**
Now you need glue. DNA ligase joins the bacterial gene into the opened plasmid by forming phosphodiester bonds, creating recombinant plasmid DNA. This recombinant plasmid is the vector that can then be introduced into soybean cells.

Adding the On Switch for Expression**
A gene from bacteria will be silent in a plant unless you add a plant promoter, a section of regulatory DNA. The promoter is where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription, so it ensures the foreign gene is expressed and the soybean plant actually becomes herbicide-resistant.

Final answer: Restriction endonuclease cuts the bacterial herbicide-resistance gene/DNA and cuts open a plasmid/vector; DNA ligase joins the bacterial gene to the plasmid/vector to form recombinant DNA; a promoter/regulatory sequence is added which ensures expression/transcription of the foreign gene.

hints: First find the area of GM soybean alone by taking 73% of 123.5 million hectares.
Then use the fact that this GM soybean area is only 50% of all GM crops to scale up to the total GM area.
walkthrough:
Calculate GM Soybean Area**
73% of the soybean area is GM. So multiply: $73/100 \times 123.5 = 90.155$ million hectares. That is just the soybean part of GM crops.

Scale Up to All GM Crops**
You are told soybeans are 50% of the total GM crop area, so the total is double the soybean value: $90.155 \times 2 = 180.31$ million hectares. Always include the unit hectares and show both steps for full credit.
Final answer: GM soybean area $= 73/100 \times 123.5 = 90.155$ million hectares; total GM crop area $= 90.155 \times 2 = 180.31$ million hectares.

hints: Think about why a farmer and a consumer might welcome GM crops - yield, cost and food supply.
Now think about direct worries for the person eating the food - allergies, residues and labelling.
Think about what happens in the field over time when pests, weeds and pollen interact with GM traits.
For a discuss answer, remember to balance both sides with two positive and two negative social points to cover all 4 marks.
walkthrough:
Positive Social Effects - More and Cheaper Food**
GM traits like herbicide resistance or insect resistance give higher yield per hectare, so more food is produced. Farmers can use less insecticide and costs fall, giving cheaper food for consumers. Less farmland is then needed, leaving more land for biodiversity and conservation.

Negative Social Effects - Health and Trust**
On the other side, people worry about new proteins causing food allergies and about greater herbicide residue left on herbicide-resistant crops. That is why many consumers mistrust GM food and argue it must be clearly labelled so they have choice.

Negative Ecological-Social Effects - Resistance and Gene Flow**
Heavy use of one herbicide or insecticidal crop selects for resistance in weeds, insects and fungi, making control harder. Pollen drift can cross-breed GM crops with organic or conventional crops, and GM plants themselves may become invasive weeds, creating conflict between neighbouring farmers.

Final answer: Any four, with balance: positives e.g. higher yield/more food per hectare, less insecticide/pesticide use, cheaper food, less land needed leaving land for conservation, improved nutritional value; negatives e.g. risk of food allergies, more herbicide residue, evolution of resistance in pests/weeds, pollen drift/cross-breeding with non-GM crops, GM crops becoming invasive weeds, consumer mistrust/need for labelling.
